ref-0acaa8cf2ae6e7e537ed.text:
DanBot can use a VBA macro embedded in an Excel file to drop the payload.
DanBot can use HTTP in C2 communication.
DanBot has been distributed within a malicious Excel attachment via spearphishing emails.
DanBot can use a scheduled task for installation.
DanBot can Base64 encode its payload.
DanBot can use use IPv4 A records and IPv6 AAAA DNS records in C2 communications.
DanBot can upload files from compromised hosts.
DanBot can download additional files to a targeted system.
DanBot can use a VBA macro to decode its payload prior to installation and execution.
ref-0acaa8cf2ae6e7e537ed.title: SecureWorks 2019, August 27 LYCEUM Takes Center Stage in Middle East Campaign Retrieved. 2019/11/19

ref-1ad716271d48c4f40280.text: Taidoor can upload data and files from a victim's machine. Taidoor has been delivered through spearphishing emails. Taidoor can perform DLL loading. Taidoor has modified the HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run key for persistence. Taidoor has downloaded additional files onto a compromised host. Taidoor has collected the MAC address of a compromised host; it can also use GetAdaptersInfo to identify network adapters. Taidoor has relied upon a victim to click on a malicious email attachment. Taidoor has used HTTP GET and POST requests for C2. Taidoor uses RC4 to encrypt the message body of HTTP content. Taidoor has the ability to use native APIs for execution including GetProcessHeap, GetProcAddress, and LoadLibrary.
ref-1ad716271d48c4f40280.title: Trend Micro. (2012). The Taidoor Campaign. Retrieved November 12, 2014.

ref-2ca36dd20eb18280088e.text: Dridex has used the OutputDebugStringW function to avoid malware analysis as part of its anti-debugging technique. Dridex has relied upon users clicking on a malicious attachment delivered through spearphishing. Dridex has used POST requests and HTTPS for C2 communications. Dridex can use multiple layers of proxy servers to hide terminal nodes in its infrastructure. Dridex has collected a list of installed software on the system. Dridex's strings are obfuscated using RC4. Dridex has collected the computer name and OS architecture information from the system. Dridex contains a backconnect module for tunneling network traffic through a victim's computer. Infected computers become part of a P2P botnet that can relay C2 traffic to other infected peers.
ref-2ca36dd20eb18280088e.title: Check Point Research. (2021, January 4). Stopping Serial Killer: Catching the Next Strike. Retrieved September 7, 2021.

ref-3dc41ad427d7e26e954d.text:
ROKRAT can use HTTP and HTTPS for command and control communication.
ROKRAT has relied upon users clicking on a malicious attachment delivered through spearphishing.
ROKRAT can check for debugging tools.
ROKRAT has been delivered via spearphishing emails that contain a malicious Hangul Office or Microsoft Word document.
ROKRAT can use a variety of API calls to execute shellcode.
ROKRAT can collect host data and specific file types.
ROKRAT can retrieve additional malicious payloads from its C2 server.
ROKRAT can capture screenshots of the infected system using the `gdi32` library.
ROKRAT has used Visual Basic for execution.
ROKRAT can use `VirtualAlloc`, `WriteProcessMemory`, and then `CreateRemoteThread` to execute shellcode within the address space of `Notepad.exe`.
ROKRAT can encrypt data prior to exfiltration by using an RSA public key.
ROKRAT can check for VMware-related files and DLLs related to sandboxes.
ROKRAT can gather the hostname and the OS version to ensure it doesn’t run on a Windows XP or Windows Server 2003 systems.
ROKRAT can decrypt strings using the victim's hostname as the key.
ROKRAT can modify the `HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Office\` registry key so it can bypass the VB object model (VBOM) on a compromised host.
ROKRAT can send collected data to cloud storage services such as PCloud.
ROKRAT can collect the username from a compromised host.
ref-3dc41ad427d7e26e954d.title: Jazi, Hossein. (2021, January 6). Retrohunting APT37: North Korean APT used VBA self decode technique to inject RokRat. Retrieved March 22, 2022.

ref-45e6963a08d880615abd.text:
StrelaStealer encrypts the payload of HTTP POST communications using the same XOR key used for the malware's DLL payload.
StrelaStealer uses XOR-encoded strings to obfuscate items.
StrelaStealer has sideloaded a DLL payload using a renamed, legitimate `msinfo32.exe` executable.
StrelaStealer automatically sends gathered email credentials following collection to command and control servers via HTTP POST.
StrelaStealer has used a renamed, legitimate `msinfo32.exe` executable to sideload the StrelaStealer payload during initial installation.
StrelaStealer has been distributed as a DLL/HTML polyglot file.
StrelaStealer has been distributed as a spearphishing attachment.
StrelaStealer relies on user execution of a malicious file for installation.
StrelaStealer has been distributed in ISO archives. StrelaStealer has been delivered in encrypted, password-protected ZIP archives.
ref-45e6963a08d880615abd.title: DCSO CyTec Blog. (2022, November 8). #ShortAndMalicious: StrelaStealer aims for mail credentials. Retrieved December 31, 2024.

ref-57a667e1457f12deddc5.text:
Emotet has relied upon users clicking on a malicious link delivered through spearphishing.
Emotet has been observed injecting in to Explorer.exe and other processes.
Emotet has relied upon users clicking on a malicious attachment delivered through spearphishing.
Emotet has been observed to hook network APIs to monitor network traffic.
ref-57a667e1457f12deddc5.title: Salvio, J.. (2014, June 27). New Banking Malware Uses Network Sniffing for Data Theft. Retrieved March 25, 2019.

ref-690f9231b07f3d4bcffb.text: Flagpro can execute malicious VBA macros embedded in .xlsm files. Flagpro has been distributed via spearphishing as an email attachment. Flagpro has been used to execute net view on a targeted system. Flagpro has the ability to wait for a specified time interval between communicating with and executing commands from C2. Flagpro can use Native API to enable obfuscation including `GetLastError` and `GetTickCount`. Flagpro has exfiltrated data to the C2 server. Flagpro has encoded bidirectional data communications between a target system and C2 server using Base64. Flagpro has dropped an executable file to the startup directory. Flagpro has relied on users clicking a malicious attachment delivered through spearphishing. Flagpro can close specific Windows Security and Internet Explorer dialog boxes to mask external connections. Flagpro can download additional malware from the C2 server. Flagpro has been used to execute the net localgroup administrators command on a targeted system. Flagpro has been used to execute the ipconfig /all command on a victim system. Flagpro can check the name of the window displayed on the system. Flagpro has been used to run the whoami command on the system. Flagpro has been used to execute `net view` to discover mapped network shares. Flagpro has been delivered within ZIP or RAR password-protected archived files. Flagpro can collect data from a compromised host, including Windows authentication information. Flagpro can communicate with its C2 using HTTP. Flagpro can check whether the target system is using Japanese, Taiwanese, or English through detection of specific Windows Security and Internet Explorer dialog. Flagpro has been used to execute netstat -ano on a compromised host. Flagpro can download malicious files with a .tmp extension and append them with .exe prior to execution. Flagpro can use `cmd.exe` to execute commands received from C2. Flagpro has been used to run the tasklist command on a compromised system.
ref-690f9231b07f3d4bcffb.title: Hada, H. (2021, December 28).  Flagpro The new malware used by BlackTech. Retrieved March 25, 2022.

ref-8f9eea5068d1e637d3a4.text:
BADFLICK has delayed communication to the actor-controlled IP address by 5 minutes.
BADFLICK has searched for files on the infected host.
BADFLICK has compressed data using the aPLib compression library.
BADFLICK has relied upon users clicking on a malicious attachment delivered through spearphishing.
BADFLICK has download files from its C2 server.
BADFLICK has been distributed via spearphishing campaigns containing malicious Microsoft Word documents.
BADFLICK has captured victim IP address details.
BADFLICK has captured victim computer name, memory space, and CPU details.
BADFLICK has uploaded files from victims' machines.
BADFLICK can decode shellcode using a custom rotating XOR cipher.
ref-8f9eea5068d1e637d3a4.title: Accenture iDefense Unit. (2019, March 5). Mudcarp's Focus on Submarine Technologies. Retrieved August 24, 2021.

ref-e217b22ef3b7bc97d2c5.text:
ZxxZ can search a compromised host to determine if it is running Windows Defender or Kasperky antivirus.
ZxxZ has relied on victims to open a malicious attachment delivered via email.
ZxxZ has used scheduled tasks for persistence and execution.
ZxxZ has been encoded to avoid detection from static analysis tools.
ZxxZ can download and execute additional files.
ZxxZ has used a XOR key to decrypt strings.
ZxxZ can search the registry of a compromised host.
ZxxZ has been distributed via spearphishing emails, usually containing a malicious RTF or Excel attachment.
ZxxZ can collect the username from a compromised host.
ZxxZ has been disguised as a Windows security update service.
ZxxZ has created a snapshot of running processes using `CreateToolhelp32Snapshot`.
ZxxZ has collected the host name and operating system product name from a compromised machine.
ZxxZ can collect data from a compromised host.
ZxxZ has used API functions such as `Process32First`, `Process32Next`, and `ShellExecuteA`.
ref-e217b22ef3b7bc97d2c5.title: Raghuprasad, C . (2022, May 11). Bitter APT adds Bangladesh to their targets. Retrieved June 1, 2022.

ref-ec3d99473a8a282e8d16.text:
Octopus has been delivered via spearsphishing emails.
Octopus has exfiltrated data to file sharing sites.
Octopus can exfiltrate files from the system using a documents collector tool.
Octopus has compressed data before exfiltrating it using a tool called Abbrevia.
Octopus has relied upon users clicking on a malicious attachment delivered through spearphishing.
ref-ec3d99473a8a282e8d16.title: Cherepanov, A. (2018, October 4). Nomadic Octopus Cyber espionage in Central Asia. Retrieved October 13, 2021.

ref-f4ba84610c63b5f3a8c9.text: Saint Bot will use the malicious file slideshow.mp4 if present to load the core API provided by ntdll.dll to avoid any hooks placed on calls to the original ntdll.dll file by endpoint detection and response or antimalware software. Saint Bot has been distributed through malicious links contained within spearphishing emails. OutSteel can automatically scan for and collect files with specific extensions. Saint Bot has relied on users to click on a malicious link delivered via a spearphishing. OutSteel attempts to download and execute Saint Bot to a statically-defined location attempting to mimic svchost: %TEMP%\\svjhost.exe. Saint Bot has attempted to bypass UAC using `fodhelper.exe` to escalate privileges. OutSteel has been distributed as a malicious attachment within a spearphishing email. OutSteel can download files from its C2 server. OutSteel can upload files from a compromised host over its C2 channel. OutSteel has used `cmd.exe` to scan a compromised host for specific file extensions. The Saint Bot loader has used API calls to spawn `MSBuild.exe` in a suspended state before injecting the decrypted Saint Bot binary into it. Saint Bot has used the command `timeout 20` to pause the execution of its initial loader. Saint Bot can run a batch script named `del.bat` to remove any Saint Bot payload-linked files from a compromise system if anti-analysis or locale checks fail. OutSteel can collect information from a compromised host. Saint Bot has run several virtual machine and sandbox checks, including checking if `Sbiedll.dll` is present in a list of loaded modules, comparing the machine name to `HAL9TH` and the user name to `JohnDoe`, and checking the BIOS version for known virtual machine identifiers. Saint Bot can download additional files onto a compromised host. OutSteel has been distributed through malicious links contained within spearphishing emails. Saint Bot can search a compromised host for specific files. OutSteel can identify running processes on a compromised host. Saint Bot has used `.vbs` scripts for execution. OutSteel has relied on a user to execute a malicious attachment delivered via spearphishing. Saint Bot has used `cmd.exe` and `.bat` scripts for execution. OutSteel was developed using the AutoIT scripting language. OutSteel can search for specific file extensions, including zipped files. Saint Bot has used PowerShell for execution. Saint Bot has enumerated running processes on a compromised host to determine if it is running under the process name `dfrgui.exe`. Saint Bot has been obfuscated to help avoid detection. OutSteel can download the Saint Bot malware for follow-on execution. OutSteel can delete itself following the successful execution of a follow-on payload. OutSteel can automatically upload collected files to its C2 server. OutSteel has relied on a user to click a malicious link within a spearphishing email. OutSteel has used HTTP for C2 communications.
